subsystems.name: Rotor
subsystems.role: an inner loop of mass circulating faster than orbital speed; its momentum is what holds the whole structure up.

subsystems.name: Stationary sheath
subsystems.role: the outer structure that sits still relative to the ground and carries tracks, power and payloads.

subsystems.name: Levitation and linear-motor system
subsystems.role: magnetically couples rotor to sheath so the net force is outward, and later accelerates payloads.

subsystems.name: Ground access
subsystems.role: cables or towers hanging from the stationary sheath let vehicles climb from the surface.

subsystems.name: Power and thermal control
subsystems.role: supplies the ring's own energy and rejects waste heat from levitation losses.
parts: solar arrays or surface power link

subsystems.name: Stabilisation and control
subsystems.role: keeps the ring from drifting or flexing as the Moon, Sun and Earth's uneven gravity tug on it.

buildSteps.title: Fix the design
buildSteps.detail: Choose altitude and plane — typically around 200–300 km up, above most atmospheric drag, and equatorially aligned if you want the sheath to hang still over fixed ground stations. Circumference is about 41,000 km.

buildSteps.title: Simulate stability
buildSteps.detail: Model how a non-orbiting ring behaves under lunar and solar perturbation. The rotor must run a few percent above orbital speed (roughly 7.8 km/s at that altitude) so the magnetic repulsion slightly exceeds gravity and lifts the sheath.

buildSteps.title: Bootstrap the first mass to orbit
buildSteps.detail: A conventional or reusable rocket places the first thin rotor strand. This is the most expensive step, so the seed is kept as light as physically possible.

buildSteps.title: Close the loop and spin it up
buildSteps.detail: Join the strand into a complete ring, then accelerate it — with electric thrusters or magnetic drive — past orbital velocity until it supports itself and any small attached loads.

buildSteps.title: Grow the rotor
buildSteps.detail: Add mass strand by strand. Once the rotor can throw payloads, use it as a mass driver to launch more material from Earth, or fetch mass from the Moon or near-Earth asteroids, so the ring partly builds itself.

buildSteps.title: Assemble the sheath
buildSteps.detail: Wrap levitation coils, structure and tracks around the now-stable rotor. The sheath needs no exotic material — it is continuously supported along its length rather than hanging from one point.

buildSteps.title: Hang access cables
buildSteps.detail: Lower tethers from the stationary sheath to ground stations and fit climbing cars, so payloads reach the ring without rockets.

buildSteps.title: Fit launchers and commission
buildSteps.detail: Install linear motors along the ring for orbital launch, then run it — one kilogram of rotor carries roughly 8 kWh of kinetic energy, and every payload launched draws that energy down and must be paid back.

prerequisites.tech: Very low-cost launch or off-Earth mass
prerequisites.why: even a light seed ring needs megatonnes eventually; reusable rockets help but are not yet cheap enough.
maglev trains run at a few hundred km/h; the ring needs contactless support and drive at kilometres per second in vacuum.
no human crew can build a 41,000 km structure; robots must assemble and weld it.
efficient, high-field magnets make levitation gaps practical and losses small.

prerequisites.tech: Dynamic stability control for a non-orbiting ring
prerequisites.why: an unsupported ring is unstable; active control at this scale has only been studied on paper.
a ring at 200 km sweeps through the debris environment and must survive small impacts for decades.

pathway.milestone: reusable launch driving down cost per kilogram, plus renewed analytical work on orbital ring dynamics
pathway.unlocks: a credible route to putting the first rotor mass in orbit.

pathway.milestone: large-scale in-space assembly and mass drivers demonstrated in orbit
pathway.unlocks: the ability to add ring mass without launching every kilogram from Earth.

pathway.milestone: a small demonstrator loop that supports itself above orbital speed
pathway.unlocks: proof that magnetic levitation at kilometres per second can be sustained.

pathway.milestone: a seed ring with hanging access cables and a linear launcher
pathway.unlocks: electrically driven, near-continuous access to orbit from the equator.

pathway.milestone: expanded rotor mass and multiple rings in different planes
pathway.unlocks: high-volume orbital transport and the industrial base for larger structures.
